drafts.after: God promises rain for the land at the right season. He sends the first rain, also called the former rain (yoreh), to start the seed growing. He sends the latter rain (malqosh) to bring the harvest to full ripeness. This farm rhythm shows how the Holy Spirit works in two outpourings. The early rain came at Pentecost and started the Christian church growing. The latter rain comes at the end of time to ripen the harvest of the earth for Christ's return. First principle: a spiritual harvest depends entirely on God pouring out his grace at the times he has set.
drafts.reason: V1 fixed: the 43-word sentence that failed the gate is split, and the longest sentence is now 20 words. V2: the colon chain is broken into one idea per sentence in plain word order. V3: salvation history, agricultural rhythm models and divine grace are replaced with everyday words. The transliterations yoreh and malqosh and the label First principle: are kept verbatim (I1).

drafts.after: God promises that after the exile and after his people turn back to him, the LORD will circumcise their hearts. Then they will love him with all their heart and soul. Paul explains that the circumcision that counts is not the outward mark in the flesh. It is the work of the Spirit in the heart. First principle: real obedience to the covenant, God's binding promise, requires God to work inside a person and make the heart new.
drafts.reason: V2: the and/because chain and the not-but clause are split into one idea per sentence. V3: regeneration and the abstract internal divine work are replaced with everyday words (God makes the heart new); covenant is glossed as God's binding promise per the frozen glossary (rule 6).

drafts.after: His body shall not remain all night upon the tree... for he that is hanged is accursed of God. That is the law about the tree. Paul reads it as good news. He says, "Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us". First principle: the Messiah, the promised King, takes the curse of the covenant, God's binding promise, onto himself. Then the blessing of Abraham can flow out to all nations.
drafts.reason: V2: the colon chain (reads the gallows-law as gospel: Christ hath redeemed...) is split into one idea per sentence. V3: gallows-law is said in plain words and Messiah is decoded in the same sentence. The unquoted KJV clause is now quoted with every word unchanged and the gloss outside it (I1); covenant is glossed per the glossary.

drafts.after: Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD. This is the foundation confession that there is only one God. It holds together the plural title Elohim and the one word echad, which speaks of a unity of more than one. Genesis 2:24 uses that same word for husband and wife becoming "one flesh". So the one God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. They are one forever and never divided. They are joined in covenant love, the love of God's binding promise, and in his one purpose to save.
drafts.reason: V2: the stacked clauses of the old second sentence and the and-chain of the old third sentence are split. V3: biblical monotheism, compound unity and redemptive purpose are replaced with everyday words; covenant is glossed per the glossary. The citation Genesis 2:24 and the quotation "one flesh" are byte-identical, and Elohim and echad are untouched (I1).

drafts.after: Moses says the LORD will raise up a Prophet like him from among their brethren. Israel must hear that Prophet. Peter, Stephen, and John all say plainly that Jesus is this Prophet. At the Transfiguration the Father confirms it by saying "Hear Him!". First principle: Christ is the final Lawgiver. He stands between God and us. He speaks for the Father.

The quotation "Hear Him!" is carried byte-identical. QUOTE-REVIEW: "Hear Him!" vs "hear ye him" (Matthew 17:5).
